doc.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How he records
summary: He treats recording like a gig, with few takes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How about how-- do you feel like you’ve recorded enough? Do you like to record, do you like to get product out there?

I love the studios, it’s one of my favorite work places. I love being in the studio, and I work fast. With a quartet or quintet or any ensemble I’m dealing with we don’t record until we know the music. Uh and it’s ready to go. And then we treat the recording process like a gig. And we don’t if it takes more than two takes there’s something wrong I think. I think you lose something. If you if-- If you want to make it like a perfect head, I’d be more interested in a perfect solo, and if you keep doing the same take over and over and over again the solos suffer, I think. And, I mean, I don’t think it, I mean if someone makes a slight error on the head I don’t think it really matters if you got a great feeling for the whole for the ensemble and the solos are fresh. And with a band like I have, like we have, we know what we’re doing. I mean the tunes have been refined on the job so it’s, you know, put the tape on and you know if we’re not if we’re not back in an hour shell the village, you know.
